blocks.text: The marked structure in the above image represents the inner layer of the optic cup, which develops into the light-sensitive neural layer of the retina.
The retina develops from the optic vesicle.
In retinal detachment there is separation of two layers of the retina (i.e., pigment and neural layers).

items.text: **Optic nerve (Option A):** is derived from optic stalk. The center of the optic cup form the optic disc where the neural retina connects with the optic stalk, transforming it into the optic nerve.
**Lens (Option B):** develops from the lens vesicle. The posterior cells of the vesicle form transparent primary lens fibers whereas the cells in the equatorial region produce secondary lens fibers.
**Retinal pigment epithelium (Option D):** is developed from the outer layer of the optic cup.

blocks.text: The accessory middle meningeal artery (also known as the pterygomeningeal artery) does not directly lie beneath the pterion. The main middle meningeal artery lies under the pterion, but the accessory artery originates from the maxillary artery and enters through the foramen ovale, supplying the dura mater and structures in the infratemporal fossa.
Pterion is located at the anterolateral fontanelle and is formed by the union of

items.text: Squamous temporal bones & Greater wing of the sphenoid.

blocks.text: At birth, this area is filled with a membrane, which typically closes by around 2 months of age, though it can sometimes be delayed until 6 months. The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs beneath the Pterion and Stem of lateral sulcus.
Injury to this area can result in extradural or epidural haemorrhage. The pterion is a frequent location for trephination (creating an opening in the skull) during surgical procedures.

items.text: **It is the meeting point of frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones (option A):** The pterion is indeed the junction where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet.

**Blow to the lateral side of the skull injures this structure (option B):** The pterion is the weakest part of the skull, and it is particularly vulnerable to injury from a lateral blow, which can lead to an epidural hematoma due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery beneath it.

**It corresponds to the site of the anterolateral fontanelle of the fetal skull (option D):** The pterion corresponds to the location of the anterolateral fontanelle (a soft spot) in the neonatal skull, which is where the frontal, parietal, and temporal bones meet.
